# Transmission, outbreaks and One Health

> *A pathogen persists only if it reaches a new host or survives in a reservoir between hosts.
> Controlling infection depends on knowing where microbes live between hosts, how they travel, and
> where transmission can be interrupted.*

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Learning objectives
- List the six links in the chain of infection, and name a measure that breaks each.
- Classify routes of transmission, and explain why respiratory particles are not divided by a fixed
  size cut-off.
- Distinguish endemic, epidemic and pandemic disease.
- Explain R₀, R and the herd immunity threshold, and calculate the threshold from R₀.
- Distinguish point-source from propagated outbreaks by their epidemic curves, and describe the steps
  of an outbreak investigation.
- Explain the One Health principle with a local example.
:::

## How infection travels {#sec-trans-spread}

### The chain of infection {#sec-trans-chain}

Transmission is usually described as a chain of six links. Each link is a point at which the chain
can be broken, so the model is most useful as a checklist for control.

::: {.flow}
1. Infectious agent
2. Reservoir
3. Portal of exit
4. Mode of transmission
5. Portal of entry
6. Susceptible host
:::

| Link | What it means | Example of breaking it |
|---|---|---|
| Infectious agent | The organism itself | Antimicrobial treatment; sterilisation |
| Reservoir | Where the organism normally lives and multiplies: people, animals, soil or water | Treating infected people; controlling infection in animals; cleaning contaminated water systems |
| Portal of exit | How it leaves the reservoir: respiratory particles, faeces, blood, skin | Covering coughs; dressing wounds |
| Mode of transmission | How it travels ([routes of transmission](#sec-trans-routes)) | Hand hygiene; safe water; mosquito control |
| Portal of entry | How it enters the next host: mouth, airway, broken skin, mucosa | Gloves; safe injection practice |
| Susceptible host | A person who can be infected | Vaccination |

From the reservoir we can predict whether eradication is possible. An organism whose only reservoir
is humans can in principle be eradicated. An organism with an animal or environmental reservoir
cannot be, because it persists whatever happens in the human population.

::: {.example}
Smallpox, whose only reservoir was humans, has been eradicated; *Burkholderia pseudomallei*, which
lives in soil and surface water, cannot be.
:::

A **zoonosis** is an infection transmitted from animals to humans. Around 60% of known human pathogen
species, and about 75% of emerging ones, are zoonotic [@taylor2001risk].

::: {.example}
In 1999, Nipah virus spread from pigs imported from Malaysia to abattoir workers in Singapore
[@paton1999nipah].
:::

### Routes of transmission {#sec-trans-routes}

An organism reaches a new host either from another host or from the environment.

::: {.concept-tree}
[Routes of transmission]{.tree-title}

- From one host to the next
  - Contact
    - Direct: from person to person, as on hands or in sexual contact (*Staphylococcus aureus* on
      hands)
    - Indirect: through a contaminated object
  - Respiratory: particles breathed out and inhaled (influenza virus)
  - Faecal–oral: organisms in faeces, swallowed in food, water or soil (eggs of *Ascaris
    lumbricoides*, which mature in soil contaminated with faeces)
  - Blood: transfusion, shared needles or a needlestick injury (HIV)
  - Vector-borne: carried by an arthropod (*Plasmodium falciparum*, carried by mosquitoes)
  - Vertical: from mother to child, before or during birth or in breast milk (HIV)
- From the environment
  - Soil and water: inhaled, swallowed or entering through broken skin (*Burkholderia
    pseudomallei*)
  - Spores of fungi that live in soil and decaying matter, inhaled
:::

A **fomite** is an inanimate object that carries organisms, such as a door handle or a shared
keyboard. A **vector** is an arthropod that carries an organism between hosts, usually a mosquito,
tick, flea or louse. Controlling the vector interrupts every infection it carries.

::: {.example}
In Singapore, dengue control acts on the mosquito vector, including the release of male mosquitoes
carrying the bacterium *Wolbachia* ([*The microbial world*](microbial-world.qmd#sec-world-harmless)).
:::

The description of the respiratory route changed during the COVID-19 pandemic. Exhaled particles span
a continuous range of sizes. The older teaching split them into **droplet** transmission, by particles
larger than about 5 µm that fall within a metre or two, and **airborne** transmission, by smaller
particles that stay suspended and can accumulate in poorly ventilated rooms. That fixed cut-off is now
recognised as too rigid [@wang2021airborne]. Control therefore combines distance with ventilation and
shorter exposure.

<div data-island="sorter" data-src="/diagrams/transmission-sorter.yml"></div>

## Spread in populations {#sec-trans-population}

### Endemic, epidemic and pandemic {#sec-trans-levels}

A disease that is **endemic** is constantly present in a population at a roughly steady level. An
**epidemic** is a sharp rise above that baseline; a **pandemic** is an epidemic across many
countries. An **outbreak** is more cases of a disease than expected in a given place and time, and
the term is usually kept for an epidemic confined to one place.

::: {.spectrum}
[How far cases exceed the expected level, and how widely]{.tree-title}

- Endemic: present at the expected level
- Epidemic: well above the expected level in one population
- Pandemic: an epidemic across many countries

[Expected level, one population]{.spectrum-end} [Far above it, worldwide]{.spectrum-end}
:::

::: {.example}
Influenza is endemic, with cases every year, but a new strain to which few people are immune can
spread across many countries as a pandemic.
:::

### Measuring how an infection spreads {#sec-trans-measures}

| Quantity | Question it answers | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Incubation period | How long between infection and symptoms? | Sets how long contacts are observed |
| Infectious period | When can this person pass it on? | May begin before symptoms, which makes control much harder |
| Basic reproduction number, R₀ | How many people does one case infect in a fully susceptible population? | A property of the organism *and* of the population |
| Effective reproduction number, R | How many does one case infect now, given immunity and control measures? | Above 1, cases grow; below 1, the outbreak shrinks |

Because R falls as immunity rises, there is a level of immunity above which an outbreak cannot sustain
itself. This **herd immunity threshold** is 1 − 1/R₀. For an organism with an R₀ of 2 it is 50%; for
a highly transmissible one with an R₀ of 12 it is above 90%, so vaccination coverage against such an
organism must be correspondingly high.

<div data-island="epidemic-sim" data-src="/diagrams/epidemic-sim.yml"></div>

In the model, the outbreak ends while susceptible people remain, because R falls below 1 before
everyone has been infected. Reducing transmission both lowers the peak and delays it, which is the
reasoning behind measures intended to keep demand within hospital capacity. When R₀ is close to 1, a
small change in it makes a large difference to the final number infected.

## Outbreaks {#sec-trans-outbreak}

### Point-source and propagated outbreaks {#sec-trans-curves}

An **epidemic curve**, a plot of cases against time of onset, indicates the type of source. Cases
from a single shared exposure form a **point-source** outbreak; cases spread from person to person
form a **propagated** outbreak.

| Outbreak | Source | Epidemic curve | How it ends |
|---|---|---|---|
| Point source | One shared exposure, such as a contaminated meal | Cases cluster within one incubation period | Once the exposure is removed, no new cases follow |
| Propagated | Each case infects others | Successive waves about one incubation period apart, each larger than the last | When R falls below 1 |

::: {.example}
At a wedding lunch, about a third of the guests began vomiting within three hours of the meal, a
single tight cluster from one shared exposure
([*Gram-positive cocci*](../bacteria/gram-positive-cocci.qmd#sec-gpc-case)).
:::

### Investigating an outbreak {#sec-trans-investigation}

Investigation follows a standard sequence:

::: {.flow}
1. Confirm and define cases
2. Describe person, place, time
3. Form a hypothesis
4. Compare exposures
5. Act to interrupt transmission
:::

The first step establishes that the excess of cases is real and sets a case definition, which
decides who is counted. Describing the cases by person, place and time suggests a hypothesis about
the source. The hypothesis is tested by comparing exposures between people who became ill and people
who did not. Action to interrupt transmission does not wait for the investigation to be complete.

::: {.example}
In London in 1854, John Snow mapped cholera deaths around the Broad Street water pump, found that
neighbours who drank other water were spared, and persuaded the parish to remove the pump handle
before the organism was known ([Practise: the Broad Street pump](#sec-trans-case)).
:::

### Hand hygiene: the evidence came first {#sec-trans-semmelweis}

In the Vienna General Hospital in the 1840s, two maternity clinics had very different death rates from
**puerperal fever**, infection after childbirth. Mortality was several times higher in the clinic
staffed by medical students, who came to deliveries from the autopsy room, than in the midwives'
clinic. Ignaz Semmelweis reasoned that something was being carried on hands from the dead to the
living, and from May 1847 required staff to wash their hands in chlorinated lime. Mortality in his
clinic fell from 11.4% in 1846 to about 1.3% in 1848 [@semmelweis1861].

Germ theory was still decades away, so Semmelweis could not say what was being carried, and his
colleagues largely rejected the finding. He acted on a route he could interrupt without knowing the
agent, as Snow did with the Broad Street pump. WHO guidance now treats hand hygiene as the primary
measure for preventing **healthcare-associated infection**, infection acquired in the course of
medical care [@who2009handhygiene].

## One Health {#sec-trans-onehealth}

**One Health** is the principle that human, animal and environmental health are interdependent, and
that infections are best understood and controlled across all three. The connections are practical:

- Most emerging infections come from animals, so surveillance in animals gives earlier warning.
- Antimicrobials used in animals select resistant bacteria that reach people through food, water and
  direct contact.
- Changes in land use, climate and travel alter where vectors can live and which animals humans meet.

::: {.example}
In 2015, an outbreak of severe group B streptococcal infection in Singapore was linked to eating raw
freshwater fish, and the strain responsible also infects farmed fish [@kalimuddin2017gbs].
:::
